paras: The Thomasville posse shooting of Bill Davis took place on Sunday night, July 5, 1903, when a marshal and five other men exchanged gunfire with Davis, a Black man, while trying to arrest him at a cabin in Thomasville. Davis escaped under fire, two posse members were slightly wounded, and whites afterward "chastised" some Black onlookers. The only known report, in the Montgomery Advertiser, called it a "battle with posse."

According to the dispatch, Davis was whipping a Black woman on a Thomasville street on Sunday night when a Mr. Wiggins tried to stop him. The paper said Davis then "cursed and abused the white people," and Wiggins reported him to Marshal J. A. McMillan.

McMillan and five other men went to the cabin where Davis was and told him at the gate that they had come to arrest him. In the posse's account, Davis answered by firing a single-barrelled breech-loading shotgun, and the men returned fire with pistols. About twenty-two shots were fired in all. When his ammunition ran out he escaped through a window while the posse pursued him and kept shooting; no wound to Davis is mentioned.

McMillan and a Mr. Guess received slight flesh wounds from small shot, and a pistol ball cut through John Parnell's hat. A large crowd of white and Black people gathered, and the dispatch said that after some Black onlookers "used insulting language to the whites," the whites "chastised some of them."
The dispatch reported that everything was quiet on Monday and that no more trouble was expected. No report of Davis's capture or of any charge was found.

The story ran as a Thomasville special on page 5 of the Montgomery Advertiser of July 8, headlined "Battle With Posse" and "Negro Defies Arrest and Fires on Officers—He Escapes." Told entirely from the white side, it cast Davis as the aggressor, itemized each white man's wounds, and presented the beating of unnamed Black bystanders as a response to their language. No other paper, white or Black, is known to have carried it, and the text names neither county nor state.
